title: Getting Started with RJ Nexus
content: Getting Started with RJ Nexus Welcome to RJ Nexus! This guide will help you set up your new CMS. Requirements Before you begin, make sure you have: - PHP >= 8.2 - MySQL Database - Composer installed Quick Installation Run the following command in your terminal: bash composer create-project rj-nexus/rj-nexus my-site

title: Installation Guide
content: Installation Guide This guide will walk you through the process of installing RJ Nexus CMS on your server. RJ Nexus is designed to be lightweight and can be installed on almost any shared hosting or VPS without requiring SSH access or complex terminal commands. Requirements Before you begin, ensure your server meets the following minimum requirements: - PHP >= 8.2 - Database: MySQL 5.7+ or MariaDB 10.3+ - Web Server: Apache or Nginx - PHP Extensions: , , , , , , , , , , > Note: RJ Nexus no longer requires the or functions to be enabled. This makes it fully compatible with highly restrictive shared hosting environments. You do not need to ask your hosting provider to change PHP settings. Step 1: Download the ZIP 1. Go to the RJ Nexus GitHub Releases page. 2. Download the latest file for the stable release. Step 2: Upload to Your Server 1. Log in to your hosting control panel (cPanel, Plesk, or your VPS file manager). 2. Navigate to your website's root directory (usually or ). 3. Upload the file you downloaded. 4. Extract the ZIP file directly in the folder. Make sure the extracted files are in the root folder, not inside another subfolder. Step 3: Run the Installer 1. title: Plugin Development
content: Plugin Development RJ Nexus features a fully isolated, modular architecture. You can extend the CMS by creating your own plugins without modifying the core codebase. Each plugin brings its own routes, views, migrations, and assets, so it can be installed, updated, or removed without touching anything else. This guide walks you through building a basic "Hello World" plugin, then shows how to add a database, assets, translations, and hooks. What You Will Learn - How a plugin is structured and discovered - How to write , a service provider, routes, a controller, and a view - How to activate and debug your plugin - How to extend it with migrations, assets, translations, and hooks - How to package and publish it Prerequisites - A working RJ Nexus installation (see the Installation Guide) - PHP 8.2+ and basic knowledge of Laravel (service providers, routes, controllers, Blade) - Access to the folder through FTP, File Manager, or your code editor > Tip: RJ Nexus includes a built-in Plugin IDE with a code editor and AI code review, so you can write and review plugin code right inside the admin panel. --- How Plugins Work When the CMS boots, it scans for folders that contain a file. For every active plugin, RJ Nexus registers the plugin's autoloader (using the value) and runs its service provider. The provider then loads the plugin's routes, views, and any hooks. Because the core is never modified, a broken or removed plugin cannot damage your site's core files. --- Plugin Directory Structure All plugins must be placed in the following directory: Each plugin has its own folder, named after its slug. A typical structure looks like this: Naming Rules | Item | Rule | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Folder / slug | Lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only | | | Namespace | PascalCase, no spaces or hyphens | | | View namespace | Same as the slug | | | Route names | Prefixed with the slug | | > Important: The folder name, the in , and the view namespace should all match. A mismatch is the most common reason a plugin does not load. --- Step 1: Create the Metadata File Every plugin requires a file. It tells RJ Nexus that the folder is a plugin and provides its essential details. Create inside your plugin folder: Field Reference | Field | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | | Yes | The display name shown in Plugins → Manage | | | Yes | Unique identifier. Must match the folder name | | | Yes | Version number using semantic versioning () | | | Yes | Your name or company | | | Yes | A short sentence describing what the plugin does | | | Yes | Root PHP namespace that maps to the folder | | | Yes | Fully qualified class name of the service provider | > Note: In JSON, the backslash must be escaped, so write between namespace parts. --- Step 2: Create the Service Provider The Service Provider is the entry point of your plugin. It loads your views and routes and registers any hooks. Create : vs : use only to bind things into the container. Use for everything that depends on other services, such as views, routes, and hooks. --- Step 3: Define Routes Create to define where your plugin's pages will be accessible. Always give your routes a name and prefix it with your plugin slug. This prevents clashes with other plugins and lets you generate links safely: --- Step 4: Create the Controller Create : Notice the double-colon syntax in . The part before is the view namespace you registered in the service provider, and the part after it is the Blade file name. --- Step 5: Create the View (Blade) Finally, create the UI for your plugin in . RJ Nexus automatically makes your plugin compatible with the theme. The admin panel uses Tailwind CSS, so you can style your page with the same utility classes used in the rest of the dashboard. --- Step 6: Activate the Plugin 1. Log in to your RJ Nexus Admin Panel. 2. Go to Plugins → Manage. 3. You will see My Awesome Plugin in the list. 4. Click Activate. Once activated, the plugin's Service Provider runs, its routes are registered, and you can open your new plugin page. > Tip: If you make changes to your plugin's routes or service providers during development, you may need to run to see the changes immediately. --- Going Further The steps above give you a working plugin. The sections below show how to build something real. Add a Database Table (Migrations) Plugins can ship their own migrations. Create a folder inside your plugin: Register the migrations in your service provider's method: Then run them: > Best practice: Always prefix your table names (for example ) so they never collide with core tables or other plugins. Implement properly so the table can be removed cleanly. Add a Model Place it at , and use it in your controller: Add Styles and Scripts Keep your plugin's assets inside the plugin folder: Publish them to a public location from your service provider: Then reference them in Blade: Add Translations RJ Nexus supports multiple languages, so make your plugin translatable from day one. Use Hooks (Filters and Actions) Hooks let your plugin change or react to core behavior without editing core files. Register them in the service provider's method using and . | Hook type | Function | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Action | | Run your code when something happens | | Filter | | Receive a value, modify it, and return it | > Note: and are placeholders. Check the list of available hooks in the core code or in the Plugin IDE for the real names. Protect Your Routes Plugin pages in the admin area should only be visible to authorized users. Wrap your routes in the appropriate middleware: Always validate user input in your controllers: --- Debugging and Troubleshooting | Problem | Likely cause | Solution | | --- | --- | --- | | Plugin does not appear in Plugins → Manage | Missing or invalid | Check the file name, valid JSON syntax (no trailing commas), and the folder location | | "Class not found" error | Namespace does not match the folder structure | Make sure in matches the PHP and that files live under | | | View namespace mismatch | Use the same name in and in | | Route returns 404 | Routes are cached or not loaded | Run and check | | Changes are not visible | Cached views, config, or routes | Run | | White screen or HTTP 500 | PHP error in your code | Check | | Plugin breaks the site after activation | Fatal error in the provider | Rename the plugin folder (for example add ) via FTP to deactivate it, then fix the error | Useful commands during development: --- Best Practices - Keep it isolated. Never edit core files. Use hooks, routes, and views to extend the CMS. - Use a unique prefix for table names, route names, config keys, and CSS classes. - Follow PSR-12 coding standards and use type hints. - Validate and escape. Validate every input and use (escaped output) in Blade. Use only for trusted HTML. - Protect admin routes with authentication and permission checks. - Make it translatable. Use translation keys instead of hard-coded text. - Clean up after yourself. Provide methods in migrations. - Version carefully. Follow semantic versioning and keep a changelog. - Do not commit secrets. Keep API keys and passwords out of your code and repository. --- Packaging and Publishing When your plugin is ready: 1. Update the version in (for example → ). 2. Test activation, deactivation, and a fresh install on a clean site. 3. Create a ZIP of the plugin folder, with at the top level of the plugin folder. 4. Publish it on GitHub. RJ Nexus delivers plugin updates through GitHub, so tag a release for each new version. Users can then install your plugin by placing it in and activating it under Plugins → Manage. --- Plugin Checklist Before you release, confirm that: - [ ] is valid and every required field is filled in - [ ] The folder name, , and view namespace match - [ ] The plugin activates and deactivates without errors - [ ] Routes are named, prefixed, and protected - [ ] Inputs are validated and output is escaped - [ ] Migrations run cleanly and have a working - [ ] Text is translatable - [ ] A README explains installation and usage --- Next Steps - Study the Form Builder plugin as a real-world example of a larger plugin - Learn how themes and RJBuilder widgets work - Use the built-in Plugin IDE for editing and AI code review - Report bugs or request features on the GitHub issue tracker
